Vermeer the Immortal
Tracing the Dutch painter’s enduring influence, free back-to-school art supplies for NYC teachers, and a glitch at a Pioneer Works exhibition is unexpectedly illuminating.

Vermeer is everywhere. Not only in the hallowed halls of museums, but also in the gentle light that streams through the window just so, or in the crisp pages of a love letter set down gently at one’s writing desk. Historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell seems to agree in Vermeer’s Afterlives , her new title tracing the Dutch painter’s enduring presence across the arts, from film to verse. Lauren Moya Ford brings us into its exquisitely illustrated pages.

In another must-read today, a glitch at Finnegan Shannon’s Pioneer Works exhibition yields insights on institutions and accessibility. “The installation’s deviation from what I expected, like disability itself, offered me a new perspective on the world,” Bryan Martin writes, “a reminder of our collective responsibility to those who live in it.”Hyperallergic Halloween is around the corner. RSVP for our art costume party with snacks and an open bar in Brooklyn on Wednesday, October 28 — members get discounted tickets!
—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor
Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places

As strange as it may sound, Johannes Vermeer’s fame is a relatively recent phenomenon. The Dutch painter known for his exquisite, enigmatic interior scenes fell into obscurity shortly after he died deeply in debt at only 43 years old in 1675. Vermeer was barely a footnote in the annals of art history until the mid-19th century, when the Parisian critic Théophile Thoré rediscovered his work. “Here’s someone we don’t know in France, and who very much deserves to be known!” the writer proclaimed in 1866. | Lauren Moya Ford
